1.pericope_label: Asa’s ten years of quiet, and the reformation he spent them on

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the rest as a result of Abijah’s great victory, the phrase being explained two verses later as having no war in those years, and the interval spent strengthening the defences of the country. He reads the commendation as the Hebrew the good and the right, an expression the next two verses define and one used later of Hezekiah; renders the objects removed as altars of the alien; and observes that the summary in Kings about taking away all the idols his fathers had made is here expanded into details, though the chronicler omits the temple prostitutes that Kings names. Of the images he prefers shattered the pillars, obelisks of a kind dedicated to Baal and symbolising the solar rays; and he adds the limit that matters, that it is clear from two later notices the high places dedicated to the worship of Jehovah were not done away with. On the closing clause he reads quiet before him as peace enjoyed under Asa’s oversight. Keil and Delitzsch identify the same objects as sun-pillars consecrated to Baal as sun-god, erected near or upon his altars, and note how much the parallel in Kings leaves out, recording only the length of the reign, the removal of the idols, and a lifelong devotion that left the high places standing; they agree on the sense of the last clause.

Henry presses the dependence of the peace on the previous reign: Abijah’s victory laid the foundation of a peace that was the reward of Asa’s piety and reformation, so that though Abijah had little religion himself he prepared the way for one that had much; had he not quieted the land, Asa could not have reformed it, for amid the din of arms the voice of law is unheard. He breaks the commendation into three, that Asa aimed at pleasing God and studied to approve himself to him, that he saw God’s eye always upon him, which helped much to keep him to what was good, and that God graciously accepted him; happy are those who walk by this rule, to do what is right not in their own eyes, nor in the eye of the world, but in the eyes of God. On the command to the people he notices the division of labour, that since the priests attended God’s altars Asa obliged the people to do their part, requiring them to seek the God of their fathers and not the gods of the heathen; and though they were much in love with their idols and very loth to leave them, the convictions of their consciences sided with the commands of Asa, so that they could not for shame refuse. He turns this into counsel for magistrates, that those who use power vigorously against profaneness meet less opposition than they feared, vice being a sneaking thing.

Wesley qualifies the word quiet, allowing no open war but private hostilities between Asa’s subjects and Baasha’s. Clarke reports the reckoning that counts the ten years from the fifth of the reign to the fifteenth, and narrows the commendation to the law’s requirement about worship, Asa being no idolater though, morally speaking, not exempt from faults; he suppressed idolatry universally and encouraged the people to worship the true God.

Gill traces the altars to a strange people, the Zidonians, Ammonites and Moabites, surviving from the time of Solomon, who built them for his wives; and he reads the images as sun images, made in the form of the sun, or dedicated to it, or temples for it. Of the command he specifies the means, that Asa did it by a public edict, requiring prayer to God and him only.

debates.question: Where did the ten years’ quiet come from, and how quiet was it?

positions.view: A result of Abijah’s great victory, the interval spent strengthening the defences
The reward of Asa’s own piety, resting on a foundation Abijah laid without religion of his own
No open war, but private hostilities between Asa’s subjects and Baasha’s
The ten years run from the fifth of the reign to the fifteenth

debates.question: How far did the reformation reach?

positions.view: Not to the high places dedicated to Jehovah, as two later notices make clear
To the sun-pillars consecrated to Baal that stood near or upon his altars
To altars left by a strange people since Solomon’s day, and to sun images
Universally, so far as idolatry went, though Asa was not himself exempt from faults

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the reformation as only possible because an irreligious predecessor had first quieted the land, and alone in drawing counsel for magistrates from the people’s compliance.
Alone in noting that the chronicler omits the temple prostitutes which the parallel in Kings names.

themes: In his days the land was quiet ten years
And Asa did that which was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God
For he took away the altars of the strange gods, and the high places, and brake down the images, and cut down the groves
And commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers, and to do the law and the commandment
Also he took away out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the images: and the kingdom was quiet before him

6.pericope_label: The fenced cities built while the land lay open, the muster of Judah and Benjamin, and Zerah’s advance

schools.summary: Ellicott admits the names of the cities are unknown and warns against the obvious guess, since Geba and Mizpah were fortified by Asa only after the war with Baasha; what is indicated here is rather a general system of defence like Rehoboam’s, who fortified fifteen cities. He notices that the word for bars, elsewhere singular, is plural here, and reads the close as meaning they built prosperously, without let or hindrance. The land being yet before them he takes to mean open to them, free from hostile occupation, a phrase borrowed from Genesis, and he notes a masculine pronoun where a feminine belongs, probably a clerical error; he would omit the word while and put a stop at bars, making the clause a statement rather than a condition: the land is still before us, for we have sought the Lord. Of the armaments he makes Judah’s the large shield and lance and Benjamin’s the short or round shield, so that the men of Judah were the hoplites, or heavy-armed, the Benjaminites the light-armed; on the total of five hundred and eighty thousand he holds the entire male population capable of bearing arms must be included, a standing army of that strength being unthinkable, and finds Benjamin’s proportion much too high. He identifies Zerah with Osorchon the Second, who succeeded Shishak, and reads the expedition as an attempt to bring Judah again under the Egyptian yoke, since Asa had restored the defences and reorganised his fighting material. Keil and Delitzsch read the muster as a foil, recorded only to show that Asa set his hope of victory not on the strength of his army but on the all-powerful help of the Lord; of Zerah they report the usual identification with Osorchon the First of the Bubastitic dynasty, but also the objection that he was an Ethiopian and no Egyptian prince who marched through Egypt as a conqueror.

Clarke states the purpose of the building plainly, to preserve his territories from invasion and strengthen the kingdom’s frontiers; guesses at the make of the arms, targets with the dagger in the centre and javelins for distant fight, and observes the second body were not only archers but carried shield and sword for close fight; and places Zerah in the Ethiopia south of Egypt near Libya, whose people are joined with his elsewhere, doubting the distance since from far off such an army could not have found forage. Wesley dwells on the rest itself, that those have rest indeed to whom God gives rest and peace indeed to whom Christ gives peace, and turns the clause about seeking into experience, that it is good to seek the Lord, since while we pursue the world we meet with nothing but vexation; of Zerah he prefers the Arabian, the Hebrew word being commonly so used and those peoples nearer.

Gill names the quarter feared in the building, a defence against Israel and other nations as Rehoboam had made before him, and suggests these were works Shishak may have demolished; he adds that the speech about building was made to the nobles and principal men. Of the arms he notes the large sort of shield that protected them and the spears to push at an enemy at close quarters. On the invading host he weighs whether these were the Cushite Arabs near Judaea or the Ethiopians of Africa, and decides for Africa, since the host included Libyans.

Henry takes the practical lesson of the muster, that Asa now found the benefit of having an army already raised against such a time of need, since provision we thought needless may soon appear of great advantage.

debates.question: How should the clause about the land being yet before us be read?

positions.view: Omit while and stop at bars: the land is still before us, for we have sought the Lord
As experience, that it is good to seek the Lord while the world yields only vexation

debates.question: What is the muster of 580,000 doing in the narrative?

positions.view: A foil: it shows Asa trusted not his army but the all-powerful help of the Lord
A census figure: the whole male population able to bear arms, with Benjamin’s share too high
A providence: he now found the benefit of an army already raised
Osorchon the Second, Shishak’s successor, come to bring Judah under the Egyptian yoke again
Usually Osorchon the First, though others make him an Ethiopian who marched through Egypt as a conqueror
Of the Ethiopia south of Egypt near Libya, though the distance makes forage a difficulty
Rather the Arabian, the Hebrew word being commonly so used and those peoples nearer
Of Africa after all, since the host included Libyans

outliers.claim: Alone in re-punctuating the building speech, and alone in classing the two tribal contingents as hoplites and light-armed.
Alone in testing the invasion against the problem of forage for so vast an army.

themes: And he built fenced cities in Judah: for the land had rest, and he had no war in those years
Let us build these cities, and make about them walls, and towers, gates, and bars, while the land is yet before us
Because we have sought the LORD our God, we have sought him, and he hath given us rest on every side. So they built and prospered
And Asa had an army of men that bare targets and spears, out of Judah three hundred thousand
And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots

10.pericope_label: Asa’s prayer in the valley at Mareshah, the rout of the Cushites, and the spoil brought back to Jerusalem

schools.summary: Ellicott admits the valley is not identified and reports the Greek reading, the ravine north of Mareshah, which would require changing a single letter in the Hebrew, while the Syriac and Arabic have the wady of Mareshah. On the central clause of the prayer he renders, there is none beside thee to help between strong and powerless, finding the construction paralleled in Genesis, and judges the alternative that makes it mean whether strong or powerless to be Rabbinic rather than ancient usage; he calls very plausible a proposal to read retain strength for help, giving, it is not for any to withstand thee, whether strong or powerless. Of the Syriac he says it is more like a Targum than a translation, evading the difficulty rather than explaining it. He adds the lexical notes: rest means rely, we go is we are come, and the word for multitude is that used of Jeroboam’s army, usually denoting an armed host. Of the pursuit he prefers survival to revival and calls the phrase a vivid hyperbole, reads before his host as before his camp since Asa’s army is the Lord’s, supposes the cities round Gerar had helped Zerah, and notes the word for spoil here is a late one where the next verse has a classical term. Keil and Delitzsch reject the identification of the valley commonly proposed and hold only that it lay nearer Mareshah, west or north-west; they render the contested clause, none is with Thee to help between a mighty one and a weak, meaning that none but God can help in an unequal battle, that is, help the weaker side, and note that the Latin took it instead to mean it makes no difference whether he helps with few or many, but hold the passage usually cited for that sense is differently worded and so no standard here. They follow the flight to Gerar, the old Philistine city whose ruins lie three leagues south-south-east of Gaza, and render the result, there fell of the Cushites so that to them was not revival, so many that they could not make a stand again.

Clarke hears in the prayer the sentiment Jonathan uttered before the garrison, and gives the Targum: help us, because we depend on thy Word, and in its name we come against this great host. Of the plunder he accounts for the quantity by position, these cities lying in the rear of the army and having laid up much forage; and of the whole affair he says the discomfiture was great because God fought for the people, though a million of men in one place is almost too much to conceive. Wesley presses the last petition, that if the enemy prevails against us he prevails as it were against thee, because thou art our God, and we go forth in thy name.

Henry draws the connection with the years of quiet, that he who sought God in his peace and prosperity could with holy boldness cry to him in his trouble and call him his God; the prayer is short, he adds, but has much in it. He breaks it into four pleas and puts the first most sharply: we do not say, Lord, take our part, for we have a good army for thee to work by, but take our part, for without thee we have no power. At the close he reads the spoil as a proverb, that the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.

Gill marks the courage of the advance, that Asa went out against him notwithstanding so great an army, and places the prayer before the battle, at the head of the army and for its encouragement. Of the last verse he reads the tents of cattle as people who dwelt in tents for the pasturage.

debates.question: What does the central clause of Asa’s prayer mean?

positions.view: There is none beside thee to help between strong and powerless — to interpose for the weaker side
None is with Thee to help between a mighty one and a weak: none but God can help in an unequal battle
The Latin sense, that it makes no difference to him whether he helps with few or with many
The sentiment Jonathan uttered before the Philistine garrison

debates.question: What is the force of the plea that man not prevail?

positions.view: If the enemy prevails against us he prevails as it were against thee, since thou art our God
Take our part not because we have a good army for thee to work by, but because without thee we have no power
Literally, let not mortal man retain strength against thee
So many fell that they could not make a stand and collect themselves again
A vivid hyperbole: they had no survival left
Great because God fought for them, though the numbers are almost too much to conceive

outliers.claim: Alone in anatomising the prayer into four distinct pleas, and alone in closing on the proverb that the sinner’s wealth is laid up for the just.
Alone in explaining the size of the spoil by the forage those rear cities had stored for the invading army.

themes: Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah
LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power
Help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude
So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled
And they smote all the cities round about Gerar; for the fear of the LORD came upon them
